why: Marco Polo (about 1254 to 1324) walks every rung of the Ladder in one real life, with a real, surprising detail at each step, and he is loved in China. Columbus is out (conquest and slavery) and Boonchu said 'No iyengar', so this replaces the Iyengar set B. Not posted before (used.txt has no Polo; the only bots-memory hit is today's planning note). Every quote is word for word from the Yule/Cordier translation (1903, Project Gutenberg 10636/12410), checked against the downloaded text; the rest is retold from Wikipedia, the Tubingen University release and the 1911 Britannica. The book's own claims (3½ years, no birds, the mountain-air cure) are told as what his book or he says, never as fact. Stakes: if you build no habit, the steps still come (getting sick, getting older, getting weaker); nobody skips them, not even the man who travelled across Asia and back, and you meet them with nothing to come back to. Why care: you are on one of these steps today. Polo got sick far from home, came back, kept learning, and near the end said he had not told half. A steady habit, same mat, same time, with a teacher who notices when you miss class, is what you carry to the next step. Open points for Boonchu: HUMAN on the cover (a kind word, a small flip: the legend was a person like us); the cover has no distance figure now (the 24,000 km was never checked against its source); RELIEF says 'He said he went too' (his claim, from one old version of his book, not a health promise); CLEAR says 'as he weakened', so it needs a from-behind photo. Source fields are internal only: never paste them into captions, comments or alt text (they hold words the content rules keep out).

caption:
Marco Polo's book tells of a plain so high and cold that no birds flew. Even he could not skip a step of life. Nobody can. But you can meet each step with a habit. Same mat, same time, and a teacher who notices when you miss class. Which step are you on right now?

left_out: The great ruler he served for about 17 years, his court, his missions for that ruler, and every word like khan, emperor, empire or Mongol (content rules; Mongol rule is also a sore subject in Russia). China is told only through what his book describes.

The war prison: Polo told his story in a Genoa prison during a Venice and Genoa war. Genoa was not his home, so the slide says 'Back in Italy, he told his story to a writer' and the credit names Rustichello of Pisa, 1298.
The sea voyage home escorting a royal bride, in which most of about 600 travellers died (royalty plus a tragedy with victims). The set just says he was away about 24 years.
The line in his will that frees 'PETER the Tartar' from bondage (slavery). Only the 'daily feebler ... sound mind' line is used, and only retold.
His mother's death (the father came home to find his wife had died): left out to keep death gentle; the quote starts at 'a son of fifteen years of age'.

Any cause for his year of illness (malaria is modern guesswork). The illness and the mountain-air cure are labelled 'one old version of his book' and credited to Ramusio's 1559 edition, as they are not in the oldest French text.
Afghanistan by name: Badakhshan is given as 'the mountains of Central Asia' to keep war associations out.
The 'did he really reach China' debate (Frances Wood, 1995): wording stays 'his book describes' and 'his book calls'. No Great Wall, tea or footbinding.

Coal ('black stones that burn') and porcelain: true and fun, but Europe already knew coal, and the slide has room for one wonder plus Hangzhou. Paper money from bark was chosen (Tubingen 2012 confirms it).
The rest of the Hangzhou passage, which names a queen, 'Bayan the conqueror' and the ruler; only 'the finest and the noblest in the world' is quoted.
Religious labels and slurs in the book ('idolaters', 'an evil race'), and the Lugou ('Marco Polo') Bridge, tied to the 1937 war.
Columbus's annotated copy of the book (Columbus is out).
The 2022 find of an earlier daughter, Agnese, from a partnership before 1300. 'He married Donata ... and they had three daughters' stays true.

The 1311 court case over musk and the 1323 house matter: they show he kept trading into his late 50s (cited in slide 9's source), but a court case reads as a fight, so the slide says 'BUSY with trade and family in Venice'.

Korcula's claim to his birth, the exact death day (8 or 9 January vs June 1324) and the book's own 'six-and-twenty years': the set says 'most likely in Venice', 'about 1254 to 1324' and 'about 24 years'.
Any portrait of Marco Polo: no real one exists, so the slides use AYBKK student photos only.

STUCK as a big word for the sick step: it is the Lane A keyword-test ask until 22 Nov. PATIENT for the cover: readers with a little English may read it as a hospital patient. The word 'journey' (banned AI word in the standing orders).

The cover's 'almost 24,000 km': Wikipedia's figure for the 1271 to 1295 trip rests on one encyclopedia (Parker 2004) that was not opened, and CLAUDE.md bars any statistic not checked against its source. The cover says 'travelled across Asia and back'.
'He learned the family trade': not in the book, and Wikipedia says almost nothing is known of his childhood before fifteen. Slide 3 says 'Little is known of his childhood'.
The full line 'things seen as seen, and things heard as heard only': old English that confuses young readers and translators. Slide 8 quotes only 'things seen' and 'things heard'.
'Friar' for Jacopo d'Acqui (a religious-order label): slide 10 calls him a chronicler and keeps 'wrote that', since Yule shows the same chronicle gets Polo's capture wrong.
TENDER for the birth step: yoga students read it as 'sore', and translators can pick the 'bid' sense next to 'traders'. GENTLE is used.

Yule's note that the missing birds on the Pamir probably mean Marco crossed late or early in the season (in summer the lake swarmed with water-fowl): too long for the slide, so slide 4 and the caption say 'his book says' and 'his book tells of' instead of stating it as fact.
